seo.title: Affiliate Marketing in Nigeria: How It Works (2026 Guide)
seo.description: A plain-English guide to affiliate marketing in Nigeria: how commission works, which programmes pay Nigerians, and how creators get paid in naira.

content.markdown:
Affiliate marketing is one of the simplest ways to earn online: you recommend a product, someone buys it through your link, and you get a cut. No stock, no delivery, no customer service.

But if you've tried it from Nigeria, you've probably hit a wall. This guide explains how affiliate marketing works, why so many programmes don't work well here, and what to look for in one that does.

## What is affiliate marketing?

Affiliate marketing is commission-based selling. A business gives you a unique link or code. When someone buys through it, the business pays you a percentage of the sale (or a fixed amount).

A simple example: a skincare brand pays 15% commission. You share a ₦20,000 serum with your followers, and 10 people buy it through your link. You earn ₦30,000, and the brand only paid for sales that actually happened.

## How affiliate marketing works, step by step

1. **You join a programme** run by a brand or a platform.
2. **You get a link** (or a code, or your own store) that tracks the sales you send.
3. **You share it** in your content: posts, stories, videos, WhatsApp status, blog.
4. **A follower buys.** The sale is tracked back to you.
5. **The commission is confirmed** after the return or refund window closes.
6. **You get paid** once you reach the payout threshold.

## Why affiliate marketing is hard in Nigeria

Most well-known affiliate programmes were built for the US and Europe. For Nigerian creators, three problems come up again and again:

- **The products don't reach your audience.** Many international stores don't ship to Nigeria, or add shipping and customs that kill the sale.
- **You can't easily receive the money.** Payouts often go through PayPal, Stripe or cheques, which many Nigerians can't use smoothly.
- **You wait months.** Some platforms hold commissions as "pending" for 30 to 120 days before they're paid.

There's also the tracking problem. Most programmes send shoppers to another website and track the sale with a cookie. If the shopper switches from their phone to a laptop, or comes back the next day, the sale can be lost.

## What to look for in an affiliate programme as a Nigerian creator

| Check | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Products your followers can buy and receive | No delivery, no sale |
| Prices in naira | Dollar prices scare shoppers away |
| Local payment options (card, transfer, USSD) | Shoppers drop off at checkout otherwise |
| Payouts to a Nigerian bank account | You actually get your money |
| Short wait before payout | You can plan around your income |
| Clear commission per product | You know what you'll earn before you post |

## ShopLink: affiliate marketing built for Nigeria

We built [ShopLink](https://shop.useaktivate.com) because Aktivate's creators kept running into these problems. Here's how it works:

- **Your own store, not just a link.** You get a storefront at `shop.useaktivate.com/@yourname`, filled with products you choose from Nigerian brands.
- **Shoppers pay on your store.** Card, transfer or USSD via Paystack, so every sale is tracked to you at checkout. No lost cookies.
- **Commission is set upfront.** Brands set rates from 5% to 50% per product, or a fixed amount, and each product shows exactly what you'll earn.
- **Paid to your bank in about a week.** Commission clears after a 7-day refund window and goes out in the next daily payout.

For a full side-by-side, read [ShopLink vs ShopMy vs LTK](https://blog.useaktivate.com/shoplink-vs-shopmy-vs-ltk).

## How to earn more from affiliate marketing

- **Only promote what you'd use.** Your audience can tell, and trust is what sells.
- **Show the product in use.** A 15-second video of you using it beats a product photo.
- **Explain why.** Add a personal note to each product in your store: "I've used this every morning for a month."
- **Keep your store focused.** Ten products that fit your niche sell better than a hundred random ones.
- **Share your link more than once.** Most sales come from repeated reminders: stories, pinned posts, WhatsApp broadcasts.
- **Time it right.** Paydays, Black Friday and December are when people buy.

## Is affiliate marketing worth it in Nigeria?

Yes, if the programme fits the market. Affiliate income starts small, but it adds up because one post can keep earning for weeks. Many creators pair it with paid brand campaigns: the campaign pays upfront, the affiliate link earns on every sale after.

**Ready to start?** [Open your ShopLink store](https://shop.useaktivate.com) and earn commission on the products you already recommend. New to Aktivate? Read [What Is ShopLink?](https://blog.useaktivate.com/what-is-shoplink) first.

content.markdown:
If you follow creator economy news, you've heard of **ShopMy** and **LTK** (formerly rewardStyle, short for LIKEtoKNOW.it). Both let creators earn commission when followers shop their recommendations, and both have paid out huge sums to creators in the US and Europe.

So why not just use them in Lagos, Nairobi or Accra? Because the details that matter most (where the products come from, how shoppers pay, and how creators get paid) were designed for a different market. This post compares them with [ShopLink](https://shop.useaktivate.com), the creator storefront we built at Aktivate for African creators and brands.

## The quick comparison

| | ShopLink | ShopMy | LTK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Built for | African creators and brands | US and global retailers | US and global retailers |
| Products | African fashion, beauty, lifestyle and FMCG brands that deliver locally | Mostly US and European retailers | Mostly US and European retailers |
| Where the shopper pays | On the creator's ShopLink store | On the retailer's website, after a redirect | On the retailer's website, after a redirect |
| Shopper payment | Card, bank transfer, USSD (Paystack) | Retailer's checkout | Retailer's checkout |
| Creator payout | Local bank account, in naira | Stripe or PayPal | PayPal or direct deposit |
| When commission is paid | After a 7-day refund window, in the next daily payout | Weekly, once commission is "locked", which can take 30–120 days | Once commission is "closed", which can take months |
| Who can join | Any creator on Aktivate; brands set their own rules | Open, with referral | By application, selective |
| Commission | Set by the brand per product, 5–50% or a fixed amount | Typically 10–30%; the creator keeps 82% | Varies by retailer |

ShopMy and LTK details are from their public help pages and reviews as of October 2026; check the sources at the end for the latest.

## 1. Products your followers can actually buy

A follower in Ikeja who taps a US retailer link often hits a store that doesn't ship to Nigeria, prices in dollars, or adds heavy shipping and customs. That sale dies at checkout, and so does your commission.

ShopLink is filled with African brands that deliver to your followers: fashion labels, beauty and skincare brands, lifestyle products and everyday goods. Prices are in naira and the brand handles delivery.

## 2. Getting paid where you live

ShopMy pays through Stripe or PayPal. LTK pays through PayPal or direct deposit. Many African creators can't receive money easily through those rails, or lose a chunk to conversion and fees when they do.

ShopLink pays your commission straight into your local bank account. Add your account once, and Nigerian accounts are verified with your bank before saving.

## 3. Getting paid fast

On ShopMy, commissions stay "pending" until the retailer pays ShopMy, which typically takes 30 to 120 days. LTK commissions have to move from "open" to "closed" first, which can also take months.

On ShopLink the shopper pays on your store, so the money is already in the system. Your commission clears after a 7-day refund window and goes out in the next daily payout. For a creator paying rent and data bills, a week versus four months is a big difference.

## 4. Every sale is tracked

ShopMy and LTK send the shopper to another website and rely on tracking cookies. If the follower switches devices, clears cookies or buys a day later from a bookmark, the sale can go untracked.

With ShopLink, the follower buys on your storefront at `shop.useaktivate.com/@yourname`. Sale, creator and commission are recorded together at checkout.

## 5. Better for brands, too

ShopMy and LTK mostly work with large retailers. ShopLink is open to African businesses of any size:

- **One-time $15 listing fee per business**, then commission only on sales.
- **Full control:** brands set the commission per product, choose whether creators can join freely, apply, or be invited, and can reward top creators with a higher rate.
- **Instant split:** the brand's share of each sale is split at checkout and settled to their bank by Paystack.
- **Access to 51,400+ verified creators** in the Aktivate network across Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa.

## What about other ways creators earn?

ShopMy and LTK aren't the only options. Here's how ShopLink fits next to the others African creators use:

- **Link-in-bio and digital product tools** (like Stan Store, Beacons or Selar) are great for selling your own e-books, courses and presets. ShopLink is for when you don't have your own product: you sell brands' products and earn commission.
- **Marketplace affiliate programmes** (like Amazon Associates or local e-commerce affiliate programmes) pay a small percentage, and the shopper leaves for a giant marketplace. On ShopLink your followers shop *your* store, curated by you, with commission rates brands set to attract creators.
- **Paid brand campaigns** pay a fixed fee for posts. They're a great income stream, and Aktivate runs one too: the Collaboration Hub. ShopLink adds income that keeps coming from every sale, long after the post goes up.

## The verdict

If you're a creator in the US with an audience that shops at Nordstrom and Sephora, ShopMy and LTK are strong choices. If your audience is in Nigeria or elsewhere in Africa, you need products they can buy, a checkout they can use and payouts you can actually receive. That's what ShopLink was built for.

seo.title: How to Make Money as a Content Creator in Nigeria (2026)
seo.description: Brand deals, affiliate sales, UGC, digital products and more. Seven ways Nigerian creators make money in 2026, and how to start each one.

content.markdown:
You post consistently, your engagement is good, and people keep saying "you should be getting paid for this." They're right. The question is *how*.

In Nigeria, creators can't always rely on the income streams creators abroad use. YouTube ad revenue is low for local audiences, and many global creator funds and affiliate programmes don't pay out here. The good news: there are more ways to earn as a Nigerian creator in 2026 than ever before, and most don't need a huge following.

Here are seven, from fastest to start to longest to build.

## 1. Paid brand campaigns

This is what most people mean by "influencer marketing." A brand pays you to create and post content about its product: a Reel, a TikTok, a story set, a review.

**How to start:**

- Make your niche obvious. Brands search by category: beauty, fashion, food, tech, finance, parenting.
- Join a campaign marketplace. On Aktivate's [Collaboration Hub](https://useaktivate.com), brands post briefs with the deliverables, budget and timeline, and creators apply.
- Fix your profile first. Brands skip creators with incomplete profiles; we wrote about [why your profile might be why brands keep skipping you](https://blog.useaktivate.com/your-profile-might-be-why-brands-keep-skipping-you).

**Good for:** creators of any size. Brands in Nigeria increasingly book **nano creators (1,000–10,000 followers)** and **micro creators (10,000–50,000)** because their audiences trust them.

## 2. Affiliate commission on sales

Instead of a fee per post, you earn a percentage of every sale you drive. It pays less upfront but keeps paying for as long as people buy.

The problem in Nigeria has been that most affiliate programmes send shoppers to foreign stores that don't deliver here, and pay through PayPal or Stripe. [ShopLink](https://shop.useaktivate.com) fixes that: you build a store of products from Nigerian brands, share one link, and get paid to your local bank account about 7 days after each sale. Brands set commissions from 5% to 50%.

Read more in [What Is ShopLink?](https://blog.useaktivate.com/what-is-shoplink)

## 3. User-generated content (UGC)

UGC creators make content that brands post on *their own* pages or use in ads. You don't need a big following, because the brand isn't paying for your audience, just your content.

**How to start:** shoot three or four sample videos for products you already own (an unboxing, a "get ready with me", an honest review) and put them in a simple portfolio. Then pitch brands directly or apply to UGC briefs.

## 4. Product gifting that turns into paid work

PR packages, where a brand sends you products to try, are often the first step to paid deals. Treat them seriously: post on time, tag the brand, and share the results with them. On ShopLink, brands can send PR packages to creators directly, and your address is only shared if you accept.

## 5. Digital products

If you teach something (makeup, editing, cooking, budgeting, fitness), package it. E-books, presets, templates, recorded classes and paid communities let you earn without a brand in the middle. Nigerian platforms like Selar make it easy to take payment in naira.

## 6. Events, hosting and appearances

Once you're known in your niche, brands and event organisers pay creators to host, attend or cover events. This is especially busy around Detty December, when lounges, restaurants, concerts and pop-ups want creators in the room.

## 7. Platform payouts

TikTok, YouTube, Facebook and Instagram all have some form of creator payout, but availability and rates for Nigerian creators vary a lot and change often. Treat platform money as a bonus, not your main income.

## Which should you start with?

| If you... | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| Make polished content but have a small following | UGC and paid campaigns |
| Get "where did you buy that?" in your DMs every day | Affiliate sales with ShopLink |
| Teach a skill people ask you about | Digital products |
| Already have strong local influence | Events and hosting |

Most full-time creators combine two or three of these. A common mix is **paid campaigns for upfront cash plus a ShopLink store for income that keeps coming** after each post.

## Five habits of creators who earn consistently

1. **Treat it like a business.** Track what you earn, from where, every month.
2. **Know your numbers.** Average views, engagement rate and audience location. Brands will ask.
3. **Reply fast.** Brands often book whoever responds first with a clear rate.
4. **Deliver on time.** One late post can cost you a repeat client.
5. **Put your links everywhere.** Bio, stories, WhatsApp status, pinned comments.

## Start today

[Join Aktivate](https://useaktivate.com) to apply for paid brand campaigns, and [open your ShopLink store](https://shop.useaktivate.com) to start earning commission from the products you already recommend. More than 51,400 creators across Nigeria, Kenya, Ghana and South Africa already have.

seo.title: How Aktivate Ran Burger King Nigeria’s Ramadan Campaign
seo.description: 7 creators, 7 posts, 14,600+ engagements. See how Aktivate ran Burger King Nigeria’s Ramadan campaign and what the data says about Muslim audiences.

content.markdown:
Ramadan is one of the biggest consumer moments of the year in Nigeria. Brands that get it right build real goodwill with a deeply engaged audience. Brands that get it wrong are easy to spot.

For Burger King Nigeria's Ramadan campaign, Aktivate picked seven creators whose audiences already trust them on faith, family, food and culture. Here's what happened, what the numbers showed, and what we'd do again.

## The Brief

Reach Nigerian Muslim audiences during Ramadan in a way that felt real, not like a sales pitch. That meant choosing creators for audience fit rather than follower count.

Each of the seven creators came from a different content area, and each published one post.

## The Creators and Their Results

[**@oyiza\_xx**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHV9-5kOGm7/) (Lifestyle) 4,201 likes, 14 comments, 13 replies. **4,228 total engagement.**

[**@mommyasa**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHN95_yty3H/) (Family & Parenting) 3,509 likes, 55 comments, 17 replies. **3,581 total engagement.**

[**@the\_aminah**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHWXq5VuYaQ/) (Lifestyle Aesthetic) 3,106 likes, 58 comments, 11 replies. **3,175 total engagement.**

[**@mayream\_salam**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHtJUJ1ohAN/) (Culture & Community) 1,795 likes, 46 comments, 7 replies. **1,848 total engagement.**

[**@feesa\_everyday**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHngq80IWgW/) (Fashion & Modesty) 995 likes, 73 comments, 27 replies. **1,095 total engagement.**

[**@angel.zee**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHoUOsVtQjX/) (Beauty) 483 likes, 215 comments, 38 replies. **736 total engagement.**

[**@shadeof.umaruu**](https://www.instagram.com/reel/DHoZrZnsyiU/) (Gen-Z / Creative) 327 likes, 13 comments, 12 replies.

**Total campaign engagement: over 14,600 from seven posts.**

## Reach Is Not the Same as Resonance

Oyiza\_xx had the highest engagement of the campaign, and almost all of it came from likes. That shows strong reach, but with only 14 comments her audience mostly watched and moved on.

Angel.zee went the other way. She had 483 likes but 215 comments, a ratio nobody else in the campaign came close to. Her audience stopped and talked back. For a campaign meant to feel culturally real, that kind of depth matters.

Feesa\_everyday sat in the middle on volume but had the second-highest comment count. Solid reach plus real conversation made her one of the most well-rounded creators on the campaign.

## Consistency Beats One Good Post

We also looked at each creator's recent posting history to separate the reliable creators from the up-and-down ones.

*   **Feesa\_everyday** averaged about 5,220 engagements per post, the highest in the group. Her campaign post came in below that, so there's room to do more with her.

*   **Mommyasa** averaged about 2,870 engagements and was the steadiest creator in the group. Her Ramadan post beat her own average.

*   **The\_aminah** averaged about 2,680 engagements, with very little change from week to week.

*   **Oyiza\_xx** averaged about 2,560 engagements across 100 posts. Her campaign post well outperformed that, so the Ramadan brief clearly landed with her audience.

*   **Mayream\_salam** spikes on faith and community content, which is exactly what a Ramadan brief needs.

*   **Angel.zee** posts less often, but her campaign post beat her average.

*   **Shadeof.umaruu** has a smaller Gen-Z audience that reliably responds to visual content.


## Why It Worked

The win came from covering several kinds of Ramadan audience at the same time.

Ramadan touches mothers planning family iftars, women shopping for modest fashion, Gen-Z creators sharing their routines, and community voices reflecting on faith. Covering all of them at once put Burger King in front of its whole potential audience, not just one slice of it.

The best performers were the creators whose audiences already linked them to Ramadan content. When a creator's own brand and the brief line up, the numbers show it.

## What We'd Do Next Time

**For long-term ambassador roles:** mommyasa, feesa\_everyday and the\_aminah. All three deliver week after week.

**For culturally specific campaigns:** mayream\_salam and mommyasa. Their comment sections show audiences who care personally.

**For maximum visibility:** oyiza\_xx and feesa\_everyday.

**For Gen-Z and niche audiences:** shadeof.umaruu and angel.zee. Smaller numbers, but very engaged communities.

## The Bigger Picture

Most brand campaigns overlook Nigeria's Muslim creators. Ramadan, with its suhoor and iftar moments, modest fashion, and family and community content, is a real chance for brands to build relationships instead of just collecting impressions.

Burger King's Ramadan campaign showed what's possible when you pair a brand with creators who already live in that culture. Over 14,600 engagements from seven posts is a strong number, and it's proof that the right creators reach people in a way they actually respond to.

* * *

*Aktivate connects Nigerian and Kenyan brands with creators whose audiences are the right fit, not just the biggest ones.* [*Get started on Aktivate*](https://useaktivate.com)*.*

seo.title: Your Profile Might Be Why Brands Keep Skipping You
seo.description: You've got good content. Your niche is clear. You're consistent. So why aren't brands booking you? More often than not, it's not the content — it's the profile.

content.markdown:
You've got good content. Your niche is clear. You're consistent. So why aren't brands booking you?

More often than not, it's not the content — it's the profile. Brands move fast when they're picking creators for a campaign, and they're scanning for a handful of specific signals before they ever look closely at your feed. Miss those signals, and you get passed over before you even get the chance to pitch.

Here are the six things brands actually check before booking a creator — and how to fix each one.

*   A complete profile


An incomplete bio, missing niche tags, or no contact information is an instant red flag. Brands don't have time to dig for information — if your profile isn't filled in fully, they'll move to the next creator who made it easy.

Fix it: Make sure your bio, niche, and contact details are all filled in and up to date. It takes ten minutes and it's often the difference between getting seen and getting skipped.

*   Verified status


Verification is a trust shortcut. Brands would rather work with a creator they know is real and active than take a chance on an unverified profile — especially when they're evaluating dozens of creators for the same campaign.

Fix it: Get verified. On most creator platforms, including Aktivate, this only takes a few minutes and immediately moves you higher in brand searches.

*   A consistent niche


Brands aren't looking for creators who can do a bit of everything. They're looking for clarity — someone whose content is recognizably about one thing, so they know exactly what kind of audience they're reaching.

Fix it: Pick a lane — beauty, gaming, travel, finance, whatever it is — and stay in it. Range might feel safer, but it makes you harder to book.

*   Recent content


An inactive feed reads as a dead account, even if you're still creating elsewhere. Brands want proof that you're active right now, not six months ago.

Fix it: Keep posting consistently, even if it's just to stay visible. Recency is a signal in itself.

*   Real engagement


Follower count gets you noticed. Engagement gets you booked. Brands increasingly look past the follower number to comments, saves, and shares — because that's what tells them your audience actually listens to you.

Fix it: Focus on content that earns comments and saves, not just views. A smaller, engaged audience will out-earn a bigger, silent one.

*   Fast response time


Campaigns move on tight timelines. A creator who takes days to reply can lose a spot to a creator who replies in hours — even if the slower creator was the better fit.

Fix it: Check your messages regularly during active campaign periods, and reply quickly. Speed is often the deciding factor between two equally qualified creators.

The takeaway

Getting booked isn't only about how good your content is — it's about how easy you make it for a brand to say yes. Fix these six things, and you remove the reasons brands have to skip you before they even get to your content.

Want the full checklist? Get matched with brand campaigns on Aktivate and start building a profile brands actually book.

seo.description: Bumpa used 2 Nigerian creators to launch their website builder. 20K+ views, sold-out intent in the comments. Here's what made it work.

content.markdown:
When Bumpa launched their website builder feature — a tool that lets Nigerian businesses create a fully functional website and drive sales directly from it — they needed to get the word out to the right audience. Not just any audience. Business owners. Entrepreneurs. People actually trying to sell things online.

Aktivate paired them with two creators who speak to exactly that community every day.

Two posts. Over 20,000 combined views. And comment sections full of people already asking how to get started.

* * *

## The Campaign Brief

Bumpa's new feature solves a real problem: most Nigerian small business owners don't have a website, and the ones that do often struggle with tools that weren't built with their reality in mind. Bumpa's website builder changes that — it's built specifically for businesses operating in Nigeria, with the infrastructure to support local sales and payments.

The goal of the campaign was simple: show real business owners that this tool exists and that it works.

* * *

## The Creators

### @hilaryodogwu — Business & Entrepreneurship

Hilary Odogwu is a trusted voice in Nigeria's online business community. Her audience comes to her for practical advice on growing a business, selling online, and navigating the tools that make it possible. When she talks about a product, her followers listen — and more importantly, they ask questions, which is exactly what happened here.

Her post generated **515 likes, 28 comments, and 14,000 views.**

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/69dcba38a84fa622cf15b3cf/d599770c-b2bb-4715-9be9-c51da41e66cb.png align="center")

### @adenikee.ruth — Business & Lifestyle

Adenike Ruth speaks to a younger, highly engaged audience of entrepreneurs and aspiring business owners. Her content style is conversational and direct, which makes brand messaging land naturally rather than feeling like an ad.

Her post generated **246 likes, 9 comments, and 6,128 plays.**

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/69dcba38a84fa622cf15b3cf/31854ddc-0457-4c30-a0a9-f119efc837c0.png align="center")

* * *

## What the Numbers Say

| Creator | Likes | Comments | Views / Plays |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| @hilaryodogwu | 515 | 28 | 14,000 |
| @adenikee.ruth | 246 | 9 | 6,128 |
| **Total** | **761** | **37** | **20,128** |

Combined, the two posts reached over 20,000 people — but the more telling signal is in the comments.

* * *

## The Comments Tell the Real Story

Engagement numbers show reach. Comments show intent.

On Hilary's post, her audience wasn't just reacting — they were already thinking about their own businesses in relation to the product. One follower asked whether someone selling cement could use the website feature. Another asked about Meta analytics integration. These aren't passive viewers. These are business owners actively evaluating whether Bumpa works for them.

That kind of comment section doesn't happen by accident. It happens when a creator has built genuine trust with an audience that takes their recommendations seriously.

Adenike's comment section told a similar story. Followers called out that a website "saves a lot of stress" and is "easier and faster." One person said they were sending the post directly to their business owner friends — which is organic word-of-mouth triggered by a single piece of creator content.

* * *

## Why This Campaign Worked

**Creator-audience fit was the foundation.** Both Hilary and Adenike have built audiences of people who are actively running or building businesses in Nigeria. Bumpa's website builder wasn't a stretch for either creator to talk about — it fits naturally into the kind of content their audiences already expect from them.

**The product is genuinely useful.** Campaigns perform best when the product solves a real problem for the creator's audience. Hilary's followers are already asking questions about online selling tools. Adenike's audience is already trying to build businesses. Bumpa's feature landed because it answered a question her audience was already asking.

**Two creators, two audiences, one message.** By working with creators in the same content vertical but with different audience profiles, the campaign reached a wider cross-section of Nigerian entrepreneurs without diluting the core message. The brief stayed consistent — the delivery felt native to each creator's style.

* * *

## The Bigger Picture

Nigeria has millions of small business owners who are selling on Instagram, WhatsApp, and in markets — but don't have a website. That gap is exactly what Bumpa is built to close. Campaigns like this one work because they meet that audience where they already are: in the comment sections of creators they trust, asking questions and looking for tools that actually work for them.

Twenty thousand views from two posts is a strong start. The comment sections suggest the message landed with exactly the right people.

posts.title: What We Learned Running Adidas Nigeria's World Cup 2026 Creator Campaign

seo.title: How Adidas Nigeria Won the World Cup with Creators
seo.description: Adidas Nigeria partnered with 6 creators for World Cup 2026. See what drove 570K+ views, real purchase intent, and viral engagement

content.markdown:
When Adidas Nigeria wanted to ride the wave of World Cup 2026 fever, they didn't reach for a traditional ad buy. They came to Aktivate's Collaboration Hub and put jerseys in the hands of six Nigerian creators with very different audiences: freestyle footballer **@chichilz**, corporate-girl comedian **@donna\_amarah**, comedian **@mc\_lively**, football personality **@playwithtomide**, style creator **@\_ivorydee**, and footballer **@oluwayinka10**.

Nine posts later, the results told a clear story: when the content feels real, the audience shows up — and they tell you exactly what they think.

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/69dcba38a84fa622cf15b3cf/ff702285-f8ca-46d8-b3b3-65dfc9801dc0.jpg align="left")

## The numbers

Across the campaign:

*   **570K+ combined views**

*   **58K+ combined likes**

*   **1,100+ comments**

*   **6 creators, 9 posts**


But raw reach only tells half the story. What made this campaign work was *why* people engaged — and that's where the comment sections got interesting.

## Comedy and relatability beat straight product shots

The single biggest performer of the campaign wasn't a polished styling post — it was **@donna\_amarah** wearing her Argentina jersey to the office and leaning all the way into the "corporate girl gone rogue" bit. That one post pulled over 400K views and nearly 41,000 likes, dwarfing everything else in the campaign.

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/69dcba38a84fa622cf15b3cf/759b1942-bc31-4789-b73e-d03f62932d59.png align="center")

**@mc\_lively** ran a similar playbook with a comedic "beef" angle — loving the jersey but refusing to betray his team loyalty — and it became one of the most *shared* posts of the campaign, with a line from his caption turning into a running joke in his own comment section.

![](https://cdn.hashnode.com/uploads/covers/69dcba38a84fa622cf15b3cf/4c8db755-33bf-4fba-b5fc-6296dd5df27e.jpg align="center")

The takeaway: audiences don't just want to see a jersey. They want a story, a bit, a reason to comment.

## Football rivalry is a built-in engagement engine

Nearly every post in the campaign turned into a mini debate — Argentina versus Spain versus France versus Portugal, Messi versus Ronaldo, club loyalties versus country loyalties. Creators didn't have to manufacture this; simply wearing a jersey was enough to invite followers to declare a side.

This rivalry energy showed up everywhere, from playful trash talk ("you go cry soon") to genuine team pride (flag emojis, "Vamos" chants) to comment sections that read like a group chat during a match. If there's one content format this campaign proved works in Nigeria, it's "let people argue about football in your comments."

## People are actually asking where to buy

Across almost every post, real purchase-intent questions showed up, unprompted:

*   "Need to get to the Adidas store"

*   "How much??"

*   "Please where can I buy Good Argentina Away jersey?"

*   "Can you tag your jersey vendor please?"


**@\_ivorydee**'s try-on post, where she sampled multiple team jerseys, generated the highest concentration of pricing and location questions in the entire campaign. People weren't just admiring the fit; they wanted to know how to get their own.

That's the kind of signal that's hard to manufacture and easy to act on.

## Sentiment was overwhelmingly positive

Across every single post, positive and playful sentiment dominated. Genuine negativity was rare and, where it appeared, usually read as banter rather than real complaint. The clearest, most useful negative signal wasn't about the creators or the brand at all — it was a handful of followers flagging that a specific jersey wasn't in stock at a specific store, which is exactly the kind of feedback a retail team can act on immediately.

## What this means for creator campaigns going forward

A few patterns are worth carrying into future briefs:

1.  **Give creators room to be funny, not just stylish.** The best-performing content wasn't the most polished — it was the most personality-driven.

2.  **Let rivalry do the work.** Team pride is a built-in conversation starter; briefs can lean into it rather than staying neutral.

3.  **Make the "where do I buy this" answer obvious.** Purchase-intent comments show up constantly — a clear link or store callout in every caption can capture that demand instead of leaving it in the comments.

4.  **Comments are a real-time retail signal.** A campaign's comment section can surface stock and availability issues faster than most internal reporting — worth treating as a feedback channel, not just a vanity metric.


World Cup fever comes around once every four years, but the lesson from this campaign travels well beyond it: audiences respond to creators being themselves, and when they do, they'll tell you — in likes, in shares, and in the comments — exactly what's working.

* * *

seo.title: How Adidas Nigeria Used a Nano Creator to Drive Black Friday
seo.description: A breakdown of Adidas Nigeria's Black Friday influencer campaign — rewatch rates, comment sentiment, purchase intent signals, and what it means for brands.

content.markdown:
## The Campaign

For its 2025 Black Friday push, Adidas Nigeria partnered with Chioma Kalu (@chiomakayy), a verified Lagos-based content creator, to drive awareness and sales both in-store and online. The campaign ran as an Instagram Reel — a ~68-second video posted in November 2025 — with a tone that felt anything but scripted.

The caption opened with: *"Not me entering adidas 'just to look' and suddenly walking out with two full bags."* No stiff ad copy. No obvious product listing. Just the kind of thing your most stylish friend might post after a shopping run.

That authenticity is the whole point — and the numbers prove it worked.

* * *

## The Numbers

| Metric | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Total video plays | 2,977 |
| Unique views | 985 |
| Likes | 189 |
| Comments | 119 |
| Avg. rewatches per viewer | ~3× |
| Comment-to-like ratio | 63% |

* * *

## Why a 3× Rewatch Rate Matters

With 985 unique viewers but 2,977 total plays, the average viewer watched this video roughly three times. That's not an accident — it's a signal that the content was genuinely entertaining, visually interesting, or both.

On Instagram's algorithm, rewatch rate is one of the strongest distribution signals available. The more a video gets rewatched, the more the algorithm interprets it as high-quality content and pushes it to new audiences. In other words, Chioma's authentic delivery didn't just perform well for existing viewers — it likely earned the brand organic reach well beyond the initial audience.

* * *

## The Comment-to-Like Ratio Tells the Real Story

A 63% comment-to-like ratio is unusually high. Most branded content sees comment rates in the low single digits as a percentage of likes. When nearly two-thirds of everyone who liked this post also left a comment, it points to a deeply activated audience — people who felt compelled to say something, not just scroll past.

The sentiment across visible comments was entirely positive:

> *"Love it 😍😍😍😍"* — @ms.efayy\_

> *"Those joggers are calling me 😍😍"* — @angie\_classy

> *"Loveeeeee"* — @kingari.x

That second comment is what brands dream about. A viewer named a specific product category and expressed purchase intent, unprompted. That's not vanity engagement. That's a conversion signal sitting right in the comments section.

* * *

## The "Drip on a Budget" Angle Hit Perfectly

The caption framed Adidas Black Friday as aspirational but accessible — *"step out looking expensive without spending too much."* For a Nigerian audience navigating real purchasing power constraints, this framing resonates far more than premium brand language ever could.

It's a positioning insight that applies broadly: African consumers aren't price-insensitive, but they are highly style-conscious. Brands that speak to both at once — quality and value — win the conversation.

* * *

## The Omnichannel Strategy Built Into the Caption

What's easy to miss is how much distribution work the caption alone did. Chioma specifically named three Adidas store locations — Circle Mall, Jakande, and Sangotedo — while also directing viewers to adidas.com/ng. One post, two conversion paths: in-store foot traffic and online sales, simultaneously.

Both @adidas and @adidasoriginals were tagged, doubling the brand touchpoints and expanding potential reach across both accounts' audiences.

* * *

## What This Means for Brands in Nigeria

The Adidas campaign with @chiomakayy is a clean case study in what works when brands trust creators to speak in their own voice. The content didn't look like an ad. It looked like something a real person posted because she genuinely went shopping and wanted to share it — which is exactly the point.

For brands looking to activate around seasonal moments like Black Friday, Ember month sales, or 9ja-specific shopping events, this approach — nano and micro creators, authentic briefs, omnichannel CTAs — consistently outperforms polished, high-production alternatives in terms of engagement depth and comment quality.

At Aktivate, this is precisely the type of campaign we were built to power: connecting the right creators with the right brands at the right moment, across Nigeria and Kenya.

posts.subtitle: A data-driven breakdown of what happened, why it worked, and what Nigerian brands can learn from it.

seo.title: How Instagram Creators Sold Out Burger King Nigeria in 1 Week
seo.description: Burger King Nigeria's Kung Fu Panda campaign generated 10,000+ engagements from just 4 posts and sold out products across multiple states in under a week.

content.markdown:
When Burger King Nigeria partnered with four Instagram creators to promote its limited-edition Kung Fu Panda menu, the results were hard to ignore — sold-out products across multiple states in under a week, increased foot traffic to locations nationwide, and over 10,000 combined interactions from just four posts.

This is a breakdown of what happened, why it worked, and what brands running influencer campaigns in Nigeria can learn from it.

* * *

## The Campaign at a Glance

The Burger King Kung Fu Panda campaign was a limited-time promotional activation tied to the film release. Four Instagram creators were selected to produce content promoting the campaign. Each creator published one post.

Four posts. Products sold out.

The creators were:

*   **@wells\_banks** — Fashion / Aesthetic

*   **@judimplez** — Storytelling / Lifestyle

*   **@mommyasa** — Family / Lifestyle

*   **@thenimichenbrand\_** — Comedy / Culture


The mix was intentional. Each creator occupied a distinct content vertical, and together they covered a wide cross-section of the Nigerian Instagram audience.

* * *

## Campaign Performance Data

Here's how the four posts performed:

| Creator | Likes | Comments | Replies | Total Engagement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| @wells\_banks | 4,452 | 49 | 17 | **4,518** |
| @judimplez | 3,097 | 131 | 131 | **3,359** |
| @mommyasa | 2,148 | 51 | 46 | **2,245** |
| @thenimichenbrand\_ | 168 | 43 | 19 | **230** |

**Total campaign engagement: 10,352**

At face value, wells\_banks dominated on total volume. But the more interesting story is in the comment and reply data — and what those numbers say about each creator's relationship with their audience.

* * *

## What the Numbers Actually Mean

### Reach vs. Resonance

Wells\_banks generated the most likes (4,452), which signals strong reach and visual pull. But judimplez generated 131 comments and 131 replies — a near-perfect 1:1 ratio that means real back-and-forth conversation was happening in the comments. That kind of engagement depth is rare, and it's the type that signals genuine audience trust.

Mommyasa sat comfortably in the mid-tier on volume but maintained a strong reply rate, pointing to an active community that goes beyond passive scrolling.

Thenimichenbrand\_ had the lowest raw numbers, but their comment-to-like ratio was the highest of the four — a clear signal of a tight-knit, highly responsive niche audience. For brands targeting Gen Z specifically, this creator's engagement quality matters more than the headline figure.

### The Right Metric Is Not Always Total Engagement

One of the clearest takeaways from this campaign is that **total engagement alone is a poor basis for creator selection**. A creator with 230 total engagements but a deeply loyal, conversion-prone audience can deliver more value per naira spent than a creator with 4,500 passive likes.

The Burger King campaign benefited from deploying all four archetypes simultaneously — which is a big part of why the products sold out.

* * *

## Historical Performance: How Consistent Were These Creators?

Looking at 26–30 posts per creator prior to the campaign reveals who was genuinely reliable:

*   **@wells\_banks and @judimplez** both averaged over 7,500 engagements per post — the strongest performers by volume

*   **@mommyasa** averaged 5,673 engagements with remarkable consistency across three months — the most reliable performer week-to-week

*   **@thenimichenbrand\_** averaged 394 engagements, but with proportionally high comment ratios indicating a loyal niche community


Consistency matters because it tells you whether a creator's campaign performance is repeatable or a one-off spike. Mommyasa's steady upward trajectory into 2025, particularly around family-oriented and seasonal content, made her the most bankable choice for a brand looking to build lasting recall.

* * *

## Why the Campaign Sold Out Products

Three factors converged to produce the sold-out result:

**1\. Creator-vertical alignment.** Each creator was matched to a content vertical that naturally fit the Burger King Kung Fu Panda brief — family fun (mommyasa), emotional storytelling (judimplez), visual aesthetics (wells\_banks), and youth humor (thenimichenbrand\_). None of the posts felt forced or out-of-character for the creator's audience.

**2\. Audience breadth with depth.** The four creators together reached parents, young adults, Gen Z, and lifestyle audiences. The campaign didn't rely on a single audience segment — it covered the full consumer profile of a fast food promotional activation.

**3\. Cultural fit.** The Kung Fu Panda IP resonated across demographics. Paired with creators whose audiences already trusted their recommendations, the product felt like a genuine discovery rather than an ad.

* * *

## What Brands Can Replicate

If you're a brand running influencer campaigns in Nigeria, here are the actionable lessons:

**Don't build your creator roster on follower count.** Wells\_banks had the highest engagement, but mommyasa had the most consistent track record. Judimplez drove the deepest conversations. Thenimichenbrand\_ owned a niche Gen Z segment nobody else touched. A one-dimensional roster built purely on follower count would have missed all of that.

**Map creators to campaign objectives, not just categories.** Product storytelling, family brand trust, fashion aesthetics, and youth humor are four different jobs. Assign creators accordingly — not interchangeably.

**Think in tiers.** This campaign used a natural tiered structure: two primary anchors for consistency and audience trust (mommyasa and judimplez), one high-visibility visual driver (wells\_banks), and one for niche reach (thenimichenbrand\_). That structure is replicable for almost any campaign brief.

**Use historical data before committing budget.** Campaign performance data is one input. Historical consistency across 26–30 posts is a far stronger predictor of whether a creator will actually deliver for your brand than a single strong post.

* * *

## Long-Term Partnership Potential

For brands looking beyond one-off activations, the data points to mommyasa and judimplez as the strongest candidates for sustained ambassador relationships. Mommyasa's consistent upward trend and content cadence make her ideal for building long-term brand recall. Judimplez's storytelling-driven engagement spikes make her the right fit for campaigns that require emotional depth and authentic voice.

Wells\_banks is best deployed for planned, high-production moments — product launches, seasonal drops, or campaigns where visual impact is the primary objective.

Thenimichenbrand\_ is an affordable route into Gen Z culture. Lower budget, lower volume, but a genuinely engaged community that responds to the right cultural brief.

* * *

## The Bigger Picture for Influencer Marketing in Nigeria

The Burger King Kung Fu Panda campaign is a useful reference point for where influencer marketing in Nigeria is heading. The days of finding someone with a large following and paying for a post are giving way to something more rigorous — creator selection based on audience fit, content vertical alignment, historical consistency, and engagement quality.

Brands that build this kind of data-driven approach to creator partnerships will consistently outperform those making selections based on follower count alone.

Four posts. Sold out in a week. That's the ceiling when the strategy is right.

If you're a brand in Nigeria or Kenya looking to run an influencer campaign, the first decision you'll make — after deciding to do it at all — is where to manage it. Do you go through an agency? Handle it manually over DMs? Or use a platform built for this?

This guide breaks down the main options available to African brands in 2026, what each one is good for, and what to watch out for. We'll also tell you where Aktivate fits in — honestly, not just as a sales pitch.

* * *

## Why the platform you choose matters

Running an influencer campaign without a proper platform is like running a payroll on WhatsApp. It works — until it doesn't. You end up with missed deadlines, payment disputes, no paper trail, and no data on what actually performed.

A good platform handles four things cleanly: finding the right creators, managing the campaign brief and approvals, paying creators on time, and reporting results. The best ones do all four without you needing a full-time coordinator to hold it together.

Here's what's available in the Nigerian and Kenyan market right now.

* * *

## 1\. Aktivate

**Best for:** Brands in Nigeria and Kenya running paid campaigns with vetted creators

Aktivate is a self-serve influencer marketing platform built specifically for the African market. Brands post a campaign — budget, deliverables, timeline — and creators from the network apply. You review applications, pick your creators, manage content approvals, and pay out through the platform.

What makes it different from the global tools is context. The creator network is Africa-first, with creators verified across Nigeria and Kenya. There's no minimum spend requirement and no subscription to get started, which makes it accessible for brands that aren't running million-naira campaigns every month.

Aktivate also powers **ShopLink** — an affiliate commerce tool for African creators, similar to ShopMy in the US. If you want to run performance-based campaigns where creators earn commission on sales they drive, that's built in.

**What it's good for:** Brands that want control without needing an agency. Startups, SMEs, and marketing teams running regular campaigns who want one place to manage everything.

**What to keep in mind:** The network is focused on Nigeria and Kenya. If you need creators across five African markets simultaneously, you may need to supplement.

**Pricing:** Campaign listing fee + 5% creator payout fee. No monthly subscription.

👉 [Start a campaign on Aktivate](https://useaktivate.com)

* * *

## 2\. Wowzi

**Best for:** Brands targeting East Africa, particularly Kenya

Wowzi is a Nairobi-based platform that has built one of the largest creator networks in East Africa, with over 200,000 creators across Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, and beyond. Brands including Coca-Cola, Safaricom, and Netflix have used it to run campaigns at scale.

Their strength is nano and micro-influencer activation at volume — they can deploy hundreds of creators simultaneously across a market, which is powerful for FMCG and telecom brands running nationwide campaigns.

**What it's good for:** Large-scale East African campaigns, particularly in Kenya. Strong on campaign automation and analytics.

**What to keep in mind:** Less suited for brands that want a hands-on, selective approach to creator partnerships. More built for volume than curation. Nigerian market coverage is limited.

* * *

## 3\. TIMA (The Influence Media Agency)

**Best for:** Brands that want full-service campaign management

TIMA is a Lagos-based influencer marketing agency with offices in Kenya, South Africa, and Ghana. Unlike self-serve platforms, TIMA handles everything — creator sourcing, briefs, content management, legal agreements, payments, and reporting. You hand them a brief and they execute.

They also handle influencer payments for foreign companies running campaigns in Nigeria, which removes a significant operational headache for international brands entering the market.

**What it's good for:** Brands with larger budgets who want zero operational lift. International brands entering Nigeria or Kenya for the first time. Multi-market African campaigns.

**What to keep in mind:** Agency model means higher cost and less direct control. Not the right fit if you want to build an in-house influencer capability over time.

* * *

## 4\. Diglancers

**Best for:** Brands wanting a self-serve creator database across multiple African markets

Diglancers is an African influencer platform and agency hybrid operating across Nigeria, South Africa, Kenya, Ghana, and several other markets. They offer a self-serve creator discovery database where brands can search, filter, and contact creators directly — as well as a managed service option.

Their positioning is broad African coverage, which is useful for brands that need to run campaigns across multiple countries without managing separate agency relationships in each.

**What it's good for:** Multi-country African campaigns. Brands that want to browse and contact creators without going through an agency every time.

**What to keep in mind:** Less established than some alternatives. Newer platform, so the creator vetting and campaign management infrastructure is still maturing.

* * *

## 5\. Global platforms (Aspire, CreatorIQ, impact.com)

**Best for:** Multinational brands with global influencer programs

Platforms like Aspire, CreatorIQ, and impact.com are the global standard for enterprise influencer marketing. They have powerful discovery tools, deep analytics, affiliate tracking, and integrations with major ad platforms.

The challenge for African brands is that these tools are built for the US and European markets. Creator databases are thin in Nigeria and Kenya. Pricing is enterprise-level — typically $500–$2,000+ per month. And the support teams have little context for African market dynamics.

**What it's good for:** Global brands running campaigns across multiple continents who need one unified platform.

**What to keep in mind:** Overkill and overpriced for most Nigerian and Kenyan brands. You'll pay for a lot of functionality you'll never use, and the African creator coverage won't justify the cost.

* * *

## Side-by-side comparison

| Platform | Africa-first | Self-serve | Managed option | Nigeria | Kenya | Pricing model |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Aktivate** | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | Per campaign + 5% fee |
| **Wowzi** | ✅ | Partial | ✅ | Limited | ✅ | Custom |
| **TIMA** | ✅ | ❌ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | Agency retainer |
| **Diglancers** | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | Custom |
| **Global platforms** | ❌ | ✅ | ❌ | Limited | Limited | $500–$2,000+/mo |

* * *

## So which one should you use?

It depends on three things: your budget, how much control you want, and which market you're operating in.

**If you're a Nigerian or Kenyan brand running regular campaigns and want to manage things yourself** — Aktivate is the most direct fit. No agency markup, no subscription, and the creator network is built for your market.

**If you're running a large East African campaign and need volume** — Wowzi's scale and automation make sense, particularly for Kenya.

**If you have budget and want someone else to handle everything** — TIMA is the most established full-service option in the Nigerian market.

**If you're an international brand entering Africa** — start with a managed service like TIMA to learn the market, then move to a self-serve platform once you have context.

**If someone is pitching you a global platform** — ask them specifically how many verified creators they have in Lagos and Nairobi before you sign anything.

* * *

## The bottom line

The African influencer marketing infrastructure is still building, which is actually an advantage for brands moving now. The cost of running campaigns on the continent is lower than in Western markets, the engagement rates are higher, and consumer trust in creators is stronger.

The platform you choose should match your stage, your budget, and how much operational lift you're willing to carry. Start simple, track everything, and scale what works.

* * *

## Ready to run your first campaign?

Aktivate connects brands in Nigeria and Kenya with vetted creators for paid campaigns — no subscription, no agency fees. Post your brief, receive creator applications, and manage approvals and payments in one place.

👉 [Post a campaign on Aktivate](https://useaktivate.com)

seo.title: What is Influencer Marketing? A Guide for African Brands
seo.description: New to influencer marketing? This plain-English guide breaks down what it is, how it works, and how brands in Nigeria and Kenya can run their first campaign.

content.markdown:
If you run a brand in Nigeria or Kenya and someone has mentioned "influencer marketing" to you in the last year, you're not alone. It's everywhere. But a lot of what's written about it is either aimed at American brands with massive budgets, or it's vague enough to be useless.

This guide is for African brands — startups, SMEs, established companies — who want to understand what influencer marketing actually is, whether it's worth it, and how to start without wasting money.

* * *

## So, what is influencer marketing?

Influencer marketing is when a brand pays a person — an influencer or creator — to promote its product or service to their audience. That audience might be on Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, X, or even WhatsApp.

The reason it works is simple: people trust other people more than they trust brands. When your favourite food creator recommends a blender, it lands differently than a billboard on the Lagos-Ibadan expressway. That trust is what you're buying when you work with an influencer.

> 53% of consumers in Kenya and Nigeria say they trust an influencer's recommendation over an ad from the brand itself.

It's not celebrity endorsement — though that's one version of it. Most influencer marketing today happens with everyday creators who have built loyal, engaged communities around a niche: food, fashion, finance, fitness, tech, parenting, entertainment. Their audiences may be smaller than a celebrity's, but they're far more responsive.

* * *

## Why it matters more in Africa than anywhere else

Traditional advertising — TV, radio, print — still exists in Nigeria and Kenya, but it's increasingly out of reach for growing brands and increasingly ignored by younger consumers. Gen Z and millennials on the continent consume content through social media, and they follow creators, not channels.

There's also a cultural dimension. African consumers respond to authenticity and community. A creator who speaks Pidgin, understands Nairobi street culture, or makes content in Yoruba reaches an audience that a globally produced brand ad simply can't. Influence in Africa is local, contextual, and deeply human.

**A few numbers worth knowing:**

*   80% of consumers in Kenya and Nigeria have bought a product after an influencer recommendation

*   Africa's creator economy is projected to exceed $17 billion by 2030, growing at ~28% annually

*   Globally, brands earn an average of $6.50 for every $1 spent on influencer marketing


* * *

## The different types of influencers

Influencers are typically grouped by follower count, but what really matters is engagement — how actively their audience responds to what they post. Here's a practical breakdown:

| Type | Followers | What to expect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Nano** | 1K – 10K | Tight-knit communities, highest engagement rates, best ROI per naira |
| **Micro** | 10K – 100K | Niche authority, consistent content, sweet spot for most campaigns |
| **Macro** | 100K – 1M | Broad reach, lower engagement, good for awareness with larger budgets |
| **Mega / Celebrity** | 1M+ | Maximum reach, minimal personal connection, best for big launches |

For most brands in Nigeria and Kenya — especially those spending under ₦5M on a campaign — nano and micro-influencers consistently deliver better results per naira. Nano influencers produce up to 49% higher engagement than micro-influencers when their content is tightly matched to the right niche.

> **Quick tip:** Don't obsess over follower count. A creator with 8,000 followers and a 12% engagement rate will drive more action for your brand than one with 200,000 followers and a 0.8% engagement rate. Always ask for engagement metrics before committing.

* * *

## What kinds of campaigns can you run?

Influencer marketing isn't one thing. Depending on your goal, you can use it in several ways:

**Product reviews and unboxings** A creator receives your product and shares their honest reaction. This works especially well for consumer goods, beauty, tech accessories, and food. Product reviews are the most influential content type among Nigerian and Kenyan consumers.

**Sponsored posts** A creator publishes a piece of content — photo, video, reel — featuring your brand with an agreed message. You define the brief; they deliver the content in their own voice.

**Affiliate campaigns** The creator gets a unique link or promo code and earns a commission on every sale they drive. This is performance-based and increasingly popular in Africa — it aligns the creator's incentive directly with your results.

**Brand ambassador programs** A longer-term partnership where a creator becomes the consistent face of your brand across multiple pieces of content. Ambassador programs deliver the highest ROI of any influencer strategy because repeated exposure builds genuine trust over time.

**Campaign activations** Tied to a specific event, product launch, or moment. You brief multiple creators simultaneously to create a wave of attention around a single campaign window.

* * *

## How does an influencer campaign actually work?

**Step 1 — Define your goal** Are you trying to drive sales, build awareness, grow your social following, or launch a new product? Your goal determines which creators to use and what content to ask for.

**Step 2 — Find the right creators** Look for creators whose audience matches your target customer — not just by demographics, but by niche and interest. A skincare brand needs beauty and lifestyle creators, not tech reviewers.

**Step 3 — Write a clear brief** Tell the creator what you want: the key message, what to include (and what to avoid), the deliverables (e.g. 1 reel + 3 stories), and the timeline. A good brief gets better content.

**Step 4 — Agree on payment terms** Negotiate a fair rate upfront. This might be a flat fee, a commission, free product, or a combination. Always confirm before content is created.

**Step 5 — Review content before it goes live** Most creators will share content for approval before posting. Check that it's on-brief and on-brand without stripping out their personality — that's what makes it effective.

**Step 6 — Track performance** Use UTM links, promo codes, or platform analytics to measure what the campaign actually drove. Reach, saves, and profile visits tell you about awareness; clicks and conversions tell you about sales impact.

* * *

## Common mistakes African brands make

**Choosing influencers by follower count alone** The number on someone's profile tells you very little. Engagement rate, audience location, content quality, and niche alignment matter far more.

**Not having a clear brief** Vague instructions produce generic content. The more specific you are about what you want communicated, the better the output — and the less back-and-forth.

**Paying for one post and expecting miracles** A single piece of content rarely moves the needle significantly. Consistent, repeated exposure from the right creator over time is what builds brand trust.

**Not tracking anything** If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. Even basic tracking — a unique discount code per creator — tells you which partnerships are working.

**Managing everything over WhatsApp and DMs** It's chaotic. It creates payment disputes, missed deadlines, and no record of what was agreed. Using a platform designed for this keeps everything clean and accountable.

* * *

## Is influencer marketing right for your brand?

Influencer marketing works best when you have a product people can actually show, a target audience that's active on social media, and a message that benefits from a trusted voice rather than a brand megaphone.

That describes most consumer-facing brands in Nigeria and Kenya right now.

If you're selling to African consumers — food, fashion, beauty, fintech, FMCG, lifestyle, e-commerce — influencer marketing isn't a nice-to-have. At this point, it's close to table stakes.

* * *

## Ready to run your first campaign?

Aktivate connects brands in Nigeria and Kenya with vetted creators for paid campaigns. Post your brief, receive applications from creators, and manage everything — briefs, approvals, and payments — in one place.

👉 [Start a campaign on Aktivate](https://useaktivate.com)
